doc.title: Jillean Williams interviewed by Milt Fillius and Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 20, 1995

chapter: Joe Williams as singer and recording artist
title: Joe's singing in the band versus solo; dancing audiences
summary: Talk of his falsetto and 'In the Evening', how many songs he sang with Basie, and how audiences once crowded the stage.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: In more different ways. The falsetto for example that famous recording of “Here’s to Life” you know I think is fantastic.

Well his party piece is “In the Evening” when he goes way up high to way down low. That always surprises people. But obviously there’s much more freedom when you’re a solo performer than when you’re with the band, you have to stick to a certain routine.
How many songs would he usually sing on a night with the Basie band?

With the Basie band it would depend on the presentation, but I would say sort of maybe five or six or something like that. Sometimes only three, depending what it was and how many shows they had to do.
Well they put in some long hours on some of those things, didn’t they?

But they would play different things. They would sometimes play dances where there was perhaps less for the singer to do. But then people always crowded ‘round the stage. People didn’t always dance then. I thought that was fun. I didn’t know that happened because we didn’t have that in England when I lived there.

I know. And the band would play and everybody just takes their partner and sort of stands up and drags them to the front of the stage. And especially when the singer is performing, you know, that gazing into their eyes, and it’s great fun. But they don’t do a lot of that anymore.
